source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2006) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R
finding: States the ACT-R utility rule: U = P*G - C, where P is the learned chance of reaching the goal, G the goal value, C the learned cost (time). Choice among matching productions is a noisy softmax over utilities.
numbers: Ui = Pi*G - Ci; P(i) = e^(Ui/t) / sum_j e^(Uj/t), t = utility noise.
limits: Textbook chapter; describes the theory, not a new experiment. G is an architectural parameter, P and C are learned.
agent_relevance: Our operator choice can use the same form: expected success times value of the goal minus cost, with noise to keep some exploration.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2006) - Lovett building-sticks task
finding: Describes Lovett's building-sticks experiment. People start with hill climbing (pick the stick closest to the goal), then switch to whatever strategy has recently worked. Four competing productions fit this: always overshoot, always undershoot, and two hill-climbing rules.
numbers: 15 problems; over 80% of participants chose overshoot on problem 5 (hill climbing favours it); by problem 7 they used overshoot always; on problems 9-11 (only undershoot works) they adapted almost at once; overshoot again on 12-14. Model started the two hill-climbing rules slightly higher, then utilities shifted with experience.
limits: Secondary description of Lovett and Anderson (1996); original not opened. Group averages over a small problem set.
agent_relevance: Success history beats surface plausibility: drop an operator quickly after it fails, and re-adopt it when the context flips.

source: Lovett & Anderson (1996) History of success and current context in problem solving
finding: Original building-sticks studies on how past success and current problem features combine in operator choice. Known here only through the secondary review above.
limits: Not opened this session; numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Founding human evidence for success-rate-based operator choice; read the original before citing numbers.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2006) - strategy discussion
finding: Utility learning is described as useful when several strategies exist for one task. The system favours the best strategy but other strategies still get sampled at a rate set by noise, so it can follow changes in the environment.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: A claim of the theory; the chapter itself notes that whether noise alone explains observed variability is open.
agent_relevance: Keep a small exploration rate in operator choice so a changed task does not lock the agent in.

source: Fu & Anderson (2006) From recurrent choice to skill learning: a reinforcement-learning model
finding: Links ACT-R utility learning to reinforcement learning (cited by the Brasoveanu and Dotlacil poster as the close connection). Not opened.
limits: Known only as a citation; no numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Utility update is a reinforcement-learning rule, so bandit tools are a fair modern substitute.

source: Brasoveanu & Dotlacil (2020) Production-based cognitive models via reinforcement learning (CUNY poster)
finding: Splits learning in production models into rule acquisition (production compilation) and rule ordering (utility estimation), and attacks ordering with Q-learning on goal-conditioned rules in lexical decision tasks of 1, 2 and 4 stimuli.
numbers: Four hand-coded rules; three task lengths; no accuracy table in the extracted poster text.
limits: Short poster, figures unreadable in text. Journal version not opened.
agent_relevance: Rule ordering by learned value is learnable; rule acquisition is the harder part, and our agent gets rules from the LLM.

source: Fitting, Evaluating, and Comparing Cognitive Architecture Models Using Likelihood: A Primer With Examples in ACT-R (2024)
finding: Gives the ACT-R reward update and shows how to fit utility learning to human choice data by likelihood. Two parameters: learning rate and utility noise.
numbers: Procedural (utility) model: alpha = 0.759, noise = 0.440, log-likelihood -30.11. Declarative model: d = 0.263, s = 0.432, log-likelihood -35.65. Procedural model fits better on one participant's gain/loss choices (win $1.0, loss -$0.5).
limits: One participant in a worked example; the authors say fit is poor for people who stay after punishment (win-shift, lose-stay).
agent_relevance: Two parameters (rate, noise) describe operator-choice learning; a good logging target for our agent.

source: Primer (2024) - stay probabilities after reward vs punishment
finding: Fitting the average stay rate hides a failure: the model cannot reproduce a person who stays after losses. Fitting both stay-after-reward and stay-after-punishment moved parameters (decay 0.12, noise 0.75) and raised likelihood only from 0.007 to 0.028.
numbers: Joint-fit L = 0.028 vs 0.007 single-measure fit; still called a poor account.
limits: Single participant; shows utility learning assumes reward-seeking, which not everyone does.
agent_relevance: Do not assume an operator-choice rule fits every case; check stay/switch rates after success and after failure.

source: Bootstrapping Cognitive Agents with a Large Language Model (2024)
finding: Builds an ACT-R and Soar style agent where the LLM writes new productions only when none applies. Productions get utilities by a Bellman backup from the 'done' action, so productions closer to success rank higher. Applicable productions are sampled by utility.
numbers: Update U_after = (N*U_before + gamma^t)/(N+1), gamma = 0.95. AI2THOR tasks find, slice, clear countertops, 15 trials each. Bootstrapped agent succeeded 15/15 on all three; action-only LLM baseline 14/15 on find, 15/15 on the others. Steps not significantly different (p = 0.446 find, 0.347 slice).
limits: Simulated kitchen only. Token and success-without-LLM columns of the table came out garbled in text extraction, so I do not quote them. High-level decisions only.
agent_relevance: Closest direct use of ACT-R-style utility in an LLM loop: reuse learned rules, ask the LLM only at impasses.

source: Bootstrapping Cognitive Agents (2024) - utility against hallucination
finding: Authors argue utility aggregation damps LLM hallucination: a bad production proposed in one context (keeps exploring after countertops are done) loses to a good production learned in another (stops when all receptacles are explored), because the good one has higher utility.
numbers: If a subtask ends in quit there is no utility update, not even a negative one, since the task may be impossible.
quote: Pgood because it is guaranteed to have a higher utility value than Pbad
limits: Argument and worked example; no ablation removing utility in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Do not punish an operator when the task was impossible; credit assignment must separate bad operator from bad world.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2023) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Maps LLM agents onto production-system cognitive architectures. The decision cycle has proposal, evaluation, selection, then execution. ReAct is called the simplest agent, with no evaluation or selection stage.
numbers: Table 2 classes agents (ReAct, Generative Agents, Tree of Thoughts, Voyager, SayCan) by which stages they use; Tree of Thoughts uses propose, evaluate, select.
limits: Position paper; no measured results. Utility learning from outcomes is not a standard part of the agents it lists.
agent_relevance: Our schema's operator choice maps to CoALA's evaluate/select step; success-rate values are the missing learned part.

source: CoALA (2023) - forms of action value
finding: Action values can come from heuristic rules, LLM perplexity (SayCan), learned values, or LLM reasoning that simulates outcomes. Selection is argmax, softmax or majority vote.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Survey statement, not a test.
agent_relevance: A cheap learned value (per-operator success counts) fits all these slots.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: LLMs in multi-armed bandits mostly fail to explore. Typical failure is a suffix failure: the best arm is never chosen again after early rounds. Only GPT-4 with a hint to explore, per-arm averages supplied by code, and chain of thought worked.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2; 72 GPT-4 configurations; hard 5-arm instance, T=100, with T=200 robustness runs. Basic GPT-4 prompt: suffix failure in more than 60% of replicates. One working configuration (buttons, suggestive framing, summarized history, reinforced CoT, temperature 0).
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Simple stationary bandits only. Authors warn external summaries may be impossible in complex tasks. 2023-24 models.
agent_relevance: Strongest warning: do not ask the LLM to track operator success in its head; keep success counts in code and show sufficient statistics.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) - second failure mode
finding: A second failure is uniform-like: the model picks all arms about equally and never narrows to the better ones. Both modes mean the LLM does not do utility learning by default.
numbers: Configuration scatter by SuffFailFreq and MinFrac; all but one configuration fail on at least one.
limits: Exact per-configuration table not readable in text form.
agent_relevance: Test our agent's operator choice for both failures: locking in too early, and never settling.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 beat humans in a multi-armed bandit but showed no sign of directed exploration (choosing the less-sampled option).
numbers: Decisions from descriptions, 13,000 problems: Davinci above chance (t(29134) = -16.85, p<.001), smaller GPT-3 models not (all p>.05), but below humans (t(29134) = -11.50, p<.001).
limits: GPT-3 era (2022); later models not tested.
agent_relevance: Learning value from experience in the prompt works somewhat, but information-seeking does not appear on its own; add it by design.

source: Schubert, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters
finding: Claude v1.3 updates value beliefs more from good than from bad surprises when it chose the option itself (optimism). The bias reverses for foregone outcomes and vanishes when someone else chooses.
numbers: Two-armed slot machines, win probabilities 0.25/0.75 etc.; positive learning rate 0.87 +/- 0.01 vs negative 0.10 +/- 0.04, t(49) = 20.1, p < .0001; asymmetric Rescorla-Wagner model posterior probability 0.93 +/- 0.04.
limits: One model (Claude v1.3), simple 2-choice task, 50 runs. Meta-RL agents show the same pattern.
agent_relevance: An LLM that tallies its own operator results will over-credit success and under-weigh failure; ACT-R's update is symmetric, so compute it outside the LLM.

source: Schubert et al. (2024) - framing effect
finding: Framing changes learning: full feedback on the unchosen option reverses the asymmetry (pessimistic for unchosen); saying another agent chose removes it.
numbers: Full-feedback blocks used reward probabilities 0.9/0.6 (high) and 0.4/0.1 (low); LLM performance improves over trials and is on par with humans.
limits: Prompt-wording dependent; effect sizes for one model.
agent_relevance: Show counterfactual outcomes of operators not chosen when we can, and phrase the log as neutral records.

source: Atalar, Zhang, Joe-Wong (2025) Neural Bandit Based Optimal LLM Selection for a Pipeline of Subtasks
finding: Treats choosing which LLM runs each pipeline step as a contextual bandit with cost, with a proof of sublinear regret. Learns without prior performance data.
numbers: Medical diagnosis set (10 runs): 7.20% higher final net reward than the best baseline (CA NeuralUCB). TeleQnA (5 runs): 7.27% over the best baseline (Random).
limits: Selects models, not reasoning operators; gains near 7% are modest and the best baseline on telecom was random choice.
agent_relevance: Expect single-digit gains, not large ones, from learned selection.

source: Life Sciences Agents with Thompson Sampling contextual bandits (2025)
finding: Thompson sampling with Beta-Bernoulli priors picks generation strategy (direct vs chain of thought), tool, or domain specialist from binary user feedback, and learns query-type rules.
numbers: After 30 queries per mode: strategy 23/30 (77%) vs random 15/30 (50%); tool 24/30 (80%) vs 14/30 (47%); domain routing 22/30 (73%) vs 15/30 (50%); average 76.7% vs 49.0%. Learned: direct answer for simple factoid 85%, chain of thought for complex mechanism 90%.
limits: Only 30 queries per mode, no confidence intervals; whether feedback was real or simulated was not verified. Industry preprint.
agent_relevance: Shows the shape of a success-rate operator selector (counts per operator per context); small numbers, treat as a demo.

source: Feng et al. (2026) Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
finding: Defines a skill utility score (specificity times abstractness) and finds tasks that retrieve higher-utility skills succeed more often.
numbers: Success rises across 10 utility bins from 14.0% to 24.5% (task-level agent) and 22.8% to 31.0% (subtask-level agent). Spearman 0.98 and 0.95, both p<0.001. Benchmarks AppWorld, OfficeBench, KramaBench.
limits: Utility is computed from text similarity, not from observed success, so it differs from ACT-R. Correlational, binned.
agent_relevance: Utility predicts success, but measured success history would be a more direct score.

source: Chen et al. (2026) SkillCraft: Can LLM Agents Learn to Use Tools Skillfully?
finding: Agents that cache and reuse verified skills save tokens, and per-skill execution success tracks task success.
numbers: Token use cut by up to 80% by skill saving and reuse; skill execution rate vs task success r = 0.65; efficiency gain vs model strength r = 0.53.
limits: Correlations across models; errors compound when skills nest.
agent_relevance: Reuse of rules that worked before is the main practical payoff of procedural memory.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) SoK: Agentic Skills
finding: Survey frames agent skills as procedural memory and cites ACT-R and Soar as formal ancestors. Covers LLM agent work from Jan 2020 to Feb 2025 plus one 2026 work.
numbers: No numbers on utility selection.
limits: Survey; framing section read only.
agent_relevance: Confirms the link from our operator set to production memory in the literature.

source: Wu, Oltramari, Francis, Giles, Ritter (2025) Cognitive LLMs: integrating cognitive architectures and LLMs for manufacturing decision-making
finding: ACT-R models generate synthetic decision traces used to fine-tune an LLM; main metric is negative log-likelihood. The review page reports only limited improvement over the pre-trained LLM.
numbers: No numeric results on the page; a reviewer calls the gains 'miniscule'. Status: accepted.
limits: Only the review page was read, not the full paper. This is training, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: ACT-R trace distillation gives small gains; supports the scaffold route over training.

source: Wei et al. (2026) FadeMem: biologically-inspired forgetting for agent memory
finding: ACT-R-adjacent decay for agent memory (not production selection). Adaptive decay with importance keeps key facts while cutting storage.
numbers: LTI-Bench after 30 days: 82.1% critical-fact retention vs Mem0 78.4% and MemGPT 75.6%, at 55.0% storage (45% reduction); multi-hop F1 falls 29.43 to 19.45 without the dual-layer memory.
limits: Declarative memory, not production selection; authors' own benchmark.
agent_relevance: Cross-link only: ACT-R-inspired decay helps memory; the production-utility side is untested there.

source: Search note (this run)
finding: Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API returned 429 rate limits, so searches used 4 WebSearch calls plus direct PDF fetches. No paper found that directly tests ACT-R utility learning in an LLM agent beyond the bootstrapping paper.
limits: Coverage gap: likely missed ICCM and MathPsych 2024-26 papers on LLMs with ACT-R.
agent_relevance: Treat 'no direct test of ACT-R utility selection in LLM loops' as probable but unverified.
